title: Waymo rider-only miles show 100% fewer bodily-injury and 76% fewer property-damage liability claims than zip-code-matched human drivers in Swiss Re claims data
summary: Over 3,868,506 rider-only miles, the Waymo Driver had no bodily-injury claims and 76% fewer property-damage claims than a Swiss Re human baseline; a later independent study found 68% fewer crashes.
account: The peer-reviewed Heliyon paper (vol. 10, issue 14, e34379) was received 25 April 2024, accepted 9 July 2024 and published 14 July 2024. Luigi Di Lillo, Xilin Zhou and Margherita Atzei (Swiss Reinsurance Company) and Tilia Gode, Ruoshu Chen and Trent Victor (Waymo LLC) wrote it. They built a human-driver baseline from over 600,000 Swiss Re property-damage and bodily-injury liability claims and 125 billion miles of exposure (claims 2016–2021). It was calibrated to Waymo One's service-area zip codes in San Francisco and Phoenix. They compared it with Waymo claims from 1 January 2018 to 1 August 2023. Over 3,868,506 rider-only miles (no human behind the wheel) Waymo had zero bodily-injury claims against a baseline of 1.11 per million miles. Waymo had 0.78 property-damage claims per million miles against 3.26, a 76% reduction. Both differences had non-overlapping 95% confidence intervals. A follow-up paper (Di Lillo, Gode, Zhou, Scanlon, Chen, Victor; not peer-reviewed) appeared on Waymo's site on 19 December 2024. It extended the data to 25.3 million fully autonomous miles (1 January 2018 to 31 July 2024) in San Francisco, Phoenix, Los Angeles and Austin. It reported 88% fewer property-damage and 92% fewer bodily-injury claims against the overall driving population (two bodily-injury claims observed against 26 expected). Against 2018–2021 model-year vehicles they were 86% and 90%. The authors note that the baseline cannot exclude freeway miles. They also note that the baseline locates each claim by the insured's registered zip code, which may differ from where the collision happened. On 16 May 2025 Waymo authors reported in Traffic Injury Prevention on 56.7 million rider-only miles through the end of January 2025. They found statistically lower any-injury, airbag-deployment and suspected-serious-injury crash rates against police-reported human benchmarks. On 23 July 2026 the Insurance Institute for Highway Safety, a research body funded by auto insurers, published an independent study by Eric Teoh, David Kidd and Luke Riexinger. Using federal crash reports from 2021 to 2024, they found that Waymo's driverless vehicles were involved in 68% fewer police-reportable crashes and 81% fewer injury crashes per mile than human drivers in the same cities. The rate was 4% higher in Austin, where the sample was small.
purpose: The Waymo Driver is built to provide driverless ride-hailing. The studies were designed to measure its liability-claim frequency against human drivers.
system: Waymo Driver (SAE Level 4 automated driving system) operating the Waymo One ride-hailing service
deployer: Waymo LLC (Waymo One in Phoenix and San Francisco; later Los Angeles and Austin)

brief: As driverless ride-hailing expands, insurance claims are one way to compare it with human driving. In a peer-reviewed paper of 14 July 2024, Swiss Re and Waymo authors reported zero bodily-injury claims over 3,868,506 driverless miles, against a human baseline of 1.11 per million miles. Waymo's property-damage claims were 0.78 per million miles against 3.26. Waymo authors co-wrote that paper and its 25-million-mile follow-up. The comparison is observational, and the authors note that the baseline cannot exclude freeway miles.[1] On 23 July 2026, the Insurance Institute for Highway Safety (IIHS) published an independent study with no Waymo authors. IIHS found that Waymo's driverless vehicles were involved in 68% fewer police-reportable crashes per mile than human drivers in the same areas. It also called for better federal data on crashes and mileage to monitor a larger rollout.[2]

fields.account: The peer-reviewed Heliyon paper (vol. 10, issue 14, e34379) was received 25 April 2024, accepted 9 July 2024 and published 14 July 2024. Luigi Di Lillo, Xilin Zhou and Margherita Atzei (Swiss Reinsurance Company) and Tilia Gode, Ruoshu Chen and Trent Victor (Waymo LLC) wrote it. They built a human-driver baseline from over 600,000 Swiss Re property-damage and bodily-injury liability claims and 125 billion miles of exposure (claims 2016–2021). It was calibrated to Waymo One's service-area zip codes in San Francisco and Phoenix. They compared it with Waymo claims from 1 January 2018 to 1 August 2023. Over 3,868,506 rider-only miles (no human behind the wheel) Waymo had zero bodily-injury claims against a baseline of 1.11 per million miles. Waymo had 0.78 property-damage claims per million miles against 3.26, a 76% reduction. Both differences had non-overlapping 95% confidence intervals. A follow-up paper (Di Lillo, Gode, Zhou, Scanlon, Chen, Victor; not peer-reviewed) appeared on Waymo's site on 19 December 2024. It extended the data to 25.3 million fully autonomous miles (1 January 2018 to 31 July 2024) in San Francisco, Phoenix, Los Angeles and Austin. It reported 88% fewer property-damage and 92% fewer bodily-injury claims against the overall driving population (two bodily-injury claims observed against 26 expected). Against 2018–2021 model-year vehicles they were 86% and 90%. The authors note that the baseline cannot exclude freeway miles. They also note that the baseline locates each claim by the insured's registered zip code, which may differ from where the collision happened. On 16 May 2025 Waymo authors reported in Traffic Injury Prevention on 56.7 million rider-only miles through the end of January 2025. They found statistically lower any-injury, airbag-deployment and suspected-serious-injury crash rates against police-reported human benchmarks. On 23 July 2026 the Insurance Institute for Highway Safety, a research body funded by auto insurers, published an independent study by Eric Teoh, David Kidd and Luke Riexinger. Using federal crash reports from 2021 to 2024, they found that Waymo's driverless vehicles were involved in 68% fewer police-reportable crashes and 81% fewer injury crashes per mile than human drivers in the same cities. The rate was 4% higher in Austin, where the sample was small.

value.text: The peer-reviewed claims comparison covered January 2018 to August 2023, and the follow-up ran through July 2024. In a separate peer-reviewed study, Waymo authors compared crash rates over 56.7 million rider-only miles through January 2025. A further study by Waymo authors, published on 28 August 2026, covered 127 million autonomous miles through September 2025. The independent study of 2021 to 2024 also found fewer crashes than human drivers in the same cities.
